| cycle | rst_n | sof | bit_in | viol after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 11 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 12 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

#### Notes
The first frame carries data bits 1, 1, 0, 1, three ones, so the parity row must deliver 1, and it delivers 0, flagging on row 7. The second frame runs out of table before its parity row, which is fine: an unarmed checker simply idles, and `sof` re-arms everything at row 8.
solution_hints: One running XOR plus a small counter carry the whole frame state between rows.
The counter distinguishes the four data positions from the single parity position; sof re-arms everything.
Even parity means the parity bit must equal the XOR of the data bits; the verdict registers for exactly that one row.

title: Checker: Valid-Ready Stability Monitor
description:
### Problem statement
Valid-ready handshakes carry one rule that separate waveforms hide: once `valid` rises, it must stay high until an edge where `ready` is also high. Dropping valid early, including on the very edge where ready first rises, means the transfer silently never happened. This monitor registers both lines and pulses `viol` for one row on any early drop.

#### Module interface
```verilog
module valid_ready_check(
    input       clk,
    input       rst_n,
    input       valid,
    input       ready,
    output reg  viol
);
```

#### Requirements
- `rst_n` is an asynchronous active-low reset that clears the delayed copies and `viol`.
- A handshake is an edge where `valid` and `ready` are both high; it frees the sender to drop `valid` afterwards.
- After an edge where `valid` was high and `ready` low, `valid` must still be high at the next edge; otherwise `viol` pulses for exactly one row.
- Dropping `valid` on the same edge `ready` first rises is still a violation, because the handshake never completed.

#### Timing table (one clock cycle per row)

| cycle | rst_n | valid | ready | viol after edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 11 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 12 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

#### Notes
Row 4 is the plain early drop. Row 11 is the sneaky one: ready rises exactly when valid falls, so no edge ever sees both high and the offer evaporates; the rule binds row 11 to row 10, not to the ready that arrives too late.
solution_hints: Remember both handshake lines from the previous row; the rule connects row k to row k+1.
A violation is exactly this: the previous row had valid high and ready low, and this row has valid low.
A completed handshake frees the sender; anything short of both lines high on the same edge keeps the obligation alive.

title: Eight-Bit Barrel Rotator
description:
### Problem statement
A barrel rotator shifts a word by a variable amount with no data loss: bits pushed off one end re-enter at the other. Rotations power circular buffers, cryptography primitives and column decoders, and unlike an arithmetic shift they never need sign extension. Here the amount is a full 3-bit field covering all eight positions.

#### Module interface
```verilog
module barrel_rot8(
    input  [7:0] d,
    input  [2:0] sh,
    output [7:0] y
);
```

#### Requirements
- `y` is `d` rotated left by `sh` positions, 0 through 7.
- Every input bit appears in the output exactly once; nothing is discarded or duplicated.
- Any combinational style is acceptable: two complementary shifts OR-ed together, or a case over `sh`.

#### Notes
A plain variable shift drops the wrapped bits; only pairing it with the complementary right shift, or enumerating the rotations in a case, makes it a rotation. Check the sh = 0 row against the pass-through case, where a careless expression often double-counts a bit.
solution_hints: A rotation re-enters the shifted-out bits at the other end; nothing is ever lost.
Shift left by sh, shift right by eight minus sh, and OR the two pieces together.
The sh = 0 row must be an exact pass-through; the complementary shift contributes nothing there.
